## Chapter 1

One day in June, 1854, the boy walked for the last time down the steps of Mr. Dixwell’s school and felt only unqualified joy. New England boys, he thought, were born too old for school; their education as men should have begun at ten. The next step was Harvard College—taken less from conviction than from custom, convenience, and economy. No one took Harvard very seriously; one went because one’s friends went, and the place stood for social self-respect.

The college that the Unitarians had tempered to moderation, balance, restraint—mesure—produced a type, not a will. Four successful years commonly left an autobiographical blank, a mind stamped with a water-mark and little else. Sometimes, in after life, Adams wondered whether education had not ruined him and most of his mates; disappointment aside, Harvard was probably less hurtful than any other university then in existence. It taught little and that little ill, but it left the mind open, free from strong prejudice, docile, ignorant.

He had looked to his class for more. The catalogue for 1854–1861 held names that were to become distinguished, and the boy felt for them as much respect then as after they rose to fame; but as help toward education, he got nothing from them and they from him. Accident counts for much in companionship, and boys bred alike have little to give one another. His class—quietly penetrating and aggressively commonplace; liberal, ironical, objectiveness itself—made the most formidable critics he would ever face. They flattered no one; they seldom praised; their judgment, like gravitation, admitted no appeal. This was Harvard incarnate; the Class of ’58 only drove the stamp deeper. Unity they had little; energy of repulsion, less. Each stood alone—easy work when one had no pains or passions.

Into this unusually dissolvent medium, chance tossed a few Southerners as unfit for it as Sioux Indians for a treadmill, and the boy’s education measured two eighteenth‑century types against each other. The Southerner had temperament rather than mind; no analytic training; no notion of admitting two ideas; but the social instinct stood him in stead, and, in legislatures, such men held their own. College was a sharper test. Vices were poor judges, yet the New Englander, even at his worst, took some care of himself; the Virginian, brooding on whiskey and grievance, might wait round the corner with a pistol. Leadership held the staff in hand; but the habit of command was not enough. The Southerner was simple beyond analysis; even simple New Englanders could not realize how childlike he was before the relative complexity of a school. Friendship, improbably, outlived political bitterness. At a time when the next ten years would kill them by scores for their college conclusions, they liked one another. The Yankee’s self‑esteem—already shading into self‑distrust—found comfort in the conviction that the slave‑holder’s strength made him weaker for modern life; but Adams began to fear that one eighteenth‑century type did not differ deeply from another. He, too, stood nearer his great‑grandfather than to a railway superintendent. An America that preferred economists to soldiers gave small welcome to either type.

If little came from mates, little more came from masters. The boy, who wanted not one‑per‑cent of an education but the whole of it—for himself alone—got barely half the average. Mathematics, the one tool he most needed to read as a universal language, never let him reach the alphabet. Ancient languages gave him two or three Greek plays; Political Economy left him a few incoherent formulas. He did not afterward remember hearing Karl Marx or Comte named. Chemistry befogged his mind with theories; only Louis Agassiz’s lectures on the Glacial Period and Paleontology stirred his curiosity more than all the rest of the instruction together. The labor of four years might have been crowded into four months of after life.

As a force, Harvard was negative, and negative forces have value. The habits it gave—no bias at all—slowly weakened his boyhood’s violent politics. The climate chained him to desultory reading till he had run through libraries he forgot even to their title‑pages; instinct led him to write; his tutors hesitated to approve, and even when he strained for recognition, they never ranked him among the first third. In this, as later, instructors gauged their scholars nearly right; when Adams himself became a professor and made mortifying mistakes in ranking others, he still clung to the school’s negative standard.

The world outside seemed large, but paths into it ran mostly through Boston, where he did not wish to go. By pure chance, the first door of escape that seemed to open led to Germany, and James Russell Lowell—who had brought back from German universities their one novelty, reading with students in his study—held it ajar. The literary world had revolted against the new money‑power; satirists scratched the middle class; critics turned to Germany for method and honesty; Goethe rose to Shakespeare; Kant outranked Plato. Lowell, no enthusiast yet convinced enough, invited his scholars to follow. Adams, caring as much to cultivate Lowell as Germany, read a little, talked more, and learned to like the contact of an older mind. He approached the Concord faith as he would a Gothic shrine—willing to admit his unworthiness if only he might pass within—but he never reached Concord. Russell Lowell was as little transcendental as Beacon Street. No revolutionary thought came; only good‑humored leave to do what amused him—two years in Europe after Cambridge.

The result was small for the effort; yet it was the only positive result Adams could trace to Harvard, and even that he doubted the college had caused. For student and president alike, the place offered chiefly what the world vulgarly called social advantages. Unluckily, social advantage was his only capital. Money he had not much; mind, not more; but his social position would never be questioned. He needed a career in which position had value; college acquaintances gave him none. The roads of life ran narrowly together; the men with whom he later bound himself—architects, artists, geologists, statesmen—did not come to him from Harvard. He would have felt more equal with them had he been less ignorant, and had he not thrown away ten years to get what he might have got in one.

The lower habits of the students did little harm; their virtues did worse. The vice of looking at life as society—an affair of the drawing‑room—strengthened a weakness that needed none. If it had made men of the world—given temper, patience, courtesy, the knack of using an opponent’s social defect—it would have been an education worth more than languages; instead, it fixed the college standard for life. Parents who sent sons to Harvard for its social uses perpetuated an inferior social type as ill‑fitted for the next generation as the Oxford type. Yet the old standard, as Walker and Lowell showed it, was admirable, and if it had little practical value, it kept a tradition for those who liked it.

Seeing that he could not succeed as a scholar, and that his social place needed no mending, Adams turned to the last remnant of old Unitarian supremacy. He took to the pen. The College Magazine printed him; the Societies listened; audiences sat grave and silent—the Harvard encouragement. He went on writing, and soon reached his limits. He could not be this or that; the very things he wanted to be. Judges always ranked him a step beneath a rival, and he believed them right. His work seemed thin, commonplace, feeble; at best, a feeling for form, an instinct of exclusion. Nothing shocked, not even its weakness.

Inevitably, effort bred ambition, and the ambition of the literary student almost took the place of scholarship’s prizes: to be chosen Class Orator. The idea lurked as a dream; he stood outside the list of popular men; yet rivals thinned, or his standing improved, till, to his own astonishment, he was elected—by a very close vote—over the first scholar, undoubtedly a better speaker and a more popular man. Politics often chose the poorer candidate; Adams was a trained politician; but he never understood how he had beaten a superior rival.

Harvard baffled him. Here were nearly a hundred young men who had lived intimately through four impressionable years, and repeatedly chose, as their representatives, precisely those least collegiate. They picked indifference to represent indifference. The successful candidate flattered himself—and them—that perhaps they were not so commonplace as they thought; but he knew they saw in him only a mirror of themselves, an infinite reflection of shortcomings. All the same, the flattery shocked his vanity; and more, because it was the only time he was ever to receive flattery of the sort.

Class Day made the Orator conspicuous. Crowded into the church, half Boston’s chaperoned youth sat in a heat to melt bronze, and listened to platitudes in clergyman’s gowns. He forgot what he said and did not care to remember; but he remembered what was said of it. An eminent uncle thought it singularly wanting in enthusiasm—perhaps a defect, perhaps the merit Harvard taught. Another elder noticed “perfect self‑possession.” Self‑possession indeed! For four years each student had figured daily before an audience that knew him to the last fibre; no future public would be so intimately intelligent. Three‑fourths of the graduates would have preferred to face the Council of Trent than the Hasty Pudding’s gala audience. This calm—teaching men to stand alone—was Harvard’s strongest gift; nothing seemed stranger to its graduates than the paroxysms of terror that seized European orators. Whether this was, or was not, education, Adams never knew. He was ready to stand before any audience in America or Europe, with nerves steadied by the excitement. Whether he would ever have anything to say remained to be proved. As yet he knew nothing. Education had not begun.

## Chapter 2

A fourth child has the strength of his weakness; being of no great value, he may throw himself away and never be missed. The parents dreaded Europe, which, they held, unfitted Americans for America; yet Boston itself offered temptations enough. The boy asked leave to begin the study of the Civil Law at a German university—no one of them knowing what the Civil Law was or why he should read it—and his indulgent father and mother consented, walking with him to the Quincy station with smiles he almost thought were tears.

He sailed in November, 1858, on the Persia, Captain Judkins’s pride; youth made the world cheerful till a heavy gale taught him, better than any university could, the meaning of a November Atlantic. No experience had less humor than sea‑sickness, but the strides in knowledge, once ashore, seemed gigantic. He learned how many impressions could be crowded into a day without making any education at all.

The Mersey gale and Liverpool murk yielded to the romance of Chester and a first awe before aristocracy at Eaton Hall. In the fifties, noble names struck a note of grandeur; gilded rooms, portraits, terraces, a landscape of superiority set the rich nobleman apart. Aristocracy was real; so was the England of Dickens, with Oliver Twist and Little Nell lurking in every churchyard shadow, and Charles the First still standing on his tower to see his army defeated. An eighteenth‑century Boston boy took it for education, and thought he felt it.

The run up to London through Birmingham and the Black District demanded a keener sense than he had. The lurid plunge into a hell of smoke and flame, and the instant glide into soft green charm, revealed an unknown society of the pit. Karl Marx waited there for him, though he did not know it. He hurried on, as he hurried from what he disliked. London itself was still London: heavy, clumsy, insular, arrogant, and not cheap. Strangers had no rights even in the Strand. History muttered down Fleet Street; Vanity Fair rolled on Piccadilly; half the great houses wore funereal hatchments; the Royal Exchange and the Bank of England were the world’s most insolent structures. He liked it best when he hated it.

Then back to the sixteenth century. As the Baron Osy steamed up the Scheldt, peasants dropped their tools and danced to a band on deck; Ostade and Teniers lived; the thirteenth‑century cathedral towered over a sixteenth‑century mass of tile and wall; Rubens was modern. The taste was thick, ripe, mediæval; he might as well have drunk it in old Malmsey for all the instruction he took. His senses woke; his reason slept.

Dropped one morning into Berlin without guide or direction, he floundered. A student at twenty takes to anything, even Berlin. Within days he was running to beer‑cellars and dance‑rooms, smoking bad tobacco, drinking poor beer, eating sauerkraut and sausage as though he knew no better. This descent was easy. When he asked for the promised education, friends led him to be registered, chose professors and courses, set him to buy the Institutes of Gaius and German tomes on the Civil Law, and took him to his first lecture.

What Berlin's Gymnasium and university failed to teach, an accidental afternoon in a beer-hall did: amid stale tobacco and Hausfrauen knitting, Beethoven's symphonic line stole into Adams's unconscious and opened a sense he had not known he possessed, even as the German drill on memory taught him its hard limits.
